deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a fair copy of lecture notes on ancient history: 'Vierter Abschnitt. Geschichte der Macedonischen Monarchie. Erster Zeitraum (800–323 a.c.)', continued from the previous page. The handwriting is German Kurrent with Latin script for proper names, and there are small blue-ink interlinear corrections. The content is as follows.
(1) Geography of Macedonia. The rivers are the Strymon, Nestus, Axius and Haliacmon. The mountains are Olympus and Pangaeus, the latter famous for its gold mines. The coastal cities are Amphipolis, Olynthus and Potidaea. The proper Macedonian cities are Pella, birthplace of Philip and Alexander, and Pydna, 'die nachherige Residenz' (the later royal residence).
(2) Beginning of the history. The history of the Macedonian monarchy properly begins only with Philip. Macedonia was inhabited by both Greeks and 'barbarians'. Around 800 BC a Hellenic colony from Argos migrated to Macedonia under the Temenids, a branch of the Heraclid family. It settled in Emathia, and the narrative continues on f.116 with the early kings and the Persian period.
The structure (period headings, date ranges, geography followed by political history) is typical of Göttingen-style universal-history lectures (cf. Heeren's handbooks). Nothing here bears on Lagrange or on any mathematical topic. The material may not even be in Gauss's own hand; it looks like a student's or copyist's notebook bound into the bundle.
errors: Historical content, not mathematical: calling Pydna 'die nachherige Residenz' is doubtful. The Macedonian royal residence moved from Aigai to Pella (under Archelaus, c. 400 BC); Pydna was never the capital. This is either a slip in the notes or a misreading.
The date of 800 BC for the Temenid migration from Argos is the traditional, legendary dating found in 18th/19th-century handbooks, not a secure historical date. This is acceptable for the genre.

results.what: Lecture notes on the geography and early history of Macedonia (rivers, mountains, cities, the Temenid/Argive foundation legend)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/19th-century German universal-history curriculum (e.g. A. H. L. Heeren, Göttingen)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical/geographical textbook material with no mathematical content. It is routine lecture-note material, possibly not even in Gauss's hand.
transcription_corrections: 'Hal{+i+}acmon' is correct: Haliacmon, with the 'i' added in blue ink.
'Pan-g{+a+}eus' = Pangaeus; the blue insertion is an 'a'.
'Poti{+d+}ea' = Potidaea; the blue correction supplies the 'd'.
'Zu den Bergen hörte' likely reads 'Zu den Bergen gehörte' (or a similar verb).
'[-mit-] {+aus+} Argos' is right: 'mit' is struck or overwritten and 'aus' is written above.
'Emathien[?]' is very likely correct (Emathia, the traditional seat of the Temenids).
The left-margin fragments ('...Alexander', '...d, wofür', etc.) belong to the facing verso page, not to f.115.
